title: Warehouses, data lakes, OLAP, batch vs stream processing
scopeHtml: Scope: OLTP vs OLAP, column stores, ETL/ELT, lakehouse, batch vs stream.

notes.title: OLTP vs OLAP
notes.html:
OLTP (online transaction processing) serves the live app: many tiny reads and writes by key. OLAP (online analytical processing) answers big questions over lots of history: few queries, each scanning millions or billions of rows.

OLTP OLAP
Example "Place order 123", "get user 42" "Revenue by city by week for 2 years"
Query touches 1 to 100 rows Millions to billions of rows, few columns
Latency goal ms seconds to minutes
Storage layout Row-oriented Column-oriented
Schema Normalized Denormalized (star schema)
Systems Postgres, MySQL, DynamoDB Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse

Running heavy analytics on the production OLTP database hurts customers: a 5-minute scan evicts cache, takes locks or I/O, and spikes latency. So you copy data to a separate analytical system.

Worked example. A 2 TB orders table. OLTP query by order id reads one 8 KB page: 1 ms. OLAP query "average order value per city for last 12 months" needs 3 columns of 500M rows. Row store reads all 2 TB; column store reads only the needed columns, about 60 GB compressed to maybe 15 GB, a 100x or more reduction in I/O.

Industry examples. Uber, Airbnb and Netflix all separate serving databases from analytical warehouses; Postgres teams offload reports to a read replica first, then to a warehouse.

Everyday analogy. A cashier serves one customer at a time quickly (OLTP); the accountant reviews the whole year's receipts in the back office (OLAP). You do not make the accountant work at the checkout counter.

Common interview traps.

  • Running reporting queries on the primary.
  • Believing one database can do both well at large scale (HTAP systems exist, such as TiDB and SingleStore, but with trade-offs).

notes.title: Column stores and the warehouse
notes.html:
A column store keeps each column's values together on disk instead of each row's. Analytics usually reads few columns of many rows, so reading only those columns saves huge I/O.

Row store (page holds whole rows):
 [1, Mumbai, 250][2, Delhi, 400][3, Mumbai, 120] ...

Column store (each column in its own file/block):
 id:    1, 2, 3 ...
 city:  Mumbai, Delhi, Mumbai ...   -> compresses extremely well
 amount:250, 400, 120 ...

Why it is fast:

  • Read only needed columns.
  • Compression: similar values compress 5x to 10x or more (dictionary encoding, run-length encoding, delta, bit-packing).
  • Vectorized execution: process batches of thousands of values with CPU SIMD.
  • Zone maps / min-max per block: skip blocks that cannot match WHERE date > ....
  • Partitioning and clustering/sort keys: prune whole partitions (for example by date).

Why it is slow for OLTP: updating one row means touching every column file; single-row lookups read blocks of many rows. Warehouses prefer bulk loads and appends.

Modern cloud warehouses separate storage and compute. Data lives in cheap object storage (S3/GCS, columnar files); compute clusters spin up on demand, scale independently and can be shared or paused. Snowflake (virtual warehouses), BigQuery (serverless slots, charged per TB scanned or by slots), Redshift (RA3 nodes with managed storage), Databricks SQL.

Star schema. A central fact table (events: orders with measures like amount, quantity and foreign keys) surrounded by dimension tables (customer, product, date, city). Queries join the big fact table to small dimensions and aggregate.

SELECT d.month, c.city, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_orders f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_id = d.date_id
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE d.year = 2026
GROUP BY d.month, c.city;

Worked example. BigQuery on-demand pricing is about $6.25 per TB scanned (confirm current price). A query selecting 3 columns from a table partitioned by date and filtered to one month scans maybe 20 GB (about $0.12); SELECT * over the whole table scans 5 TB (about $31). That is why partition filters and column selection matter.

Industry examples. Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse (used by Cloudflare and Uber for logs and analytics), Apache Druid and Pinot (low-latency real-time OLAP, used by LinkedIn and Uber for user-facing analytics).

Decision gravity. Choosing a managed warehouse is moderately reversible if you keep raw data in open formats (Parquet) in your own object store; locking everything inside a vendor format is harder to leave. Modeling (star schema, partitioning keys) is the long-lived decision.

Everyday analogy. A spreadsheet where you can read the whole "price" column in one go, instead of paging through every row card by card.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that warehouses are bad at single-row updates and high-concurrency point reads.
  • SELECT * on columnar engines.
  • No partition pruning, scanning years of data for a daily report.

notes.title: ETL, ELT and data pipelines
notes.html:
A pipeline moves data from sources (OLTP databases, event streams, SaaS tools) into the warehouse or lake and shapes it for analysis.

  • ETL: Extract, Transform, then Load; transformation happens on a separate engine (Spark, Informatica) before the warehouse. Older, good when the warehouse is expensive or data must be cleaned or masked first.
  • ELT: Extract, Load raw data, Transform inside the warehouse with SQL (dbt). Standard today because warehouses are cheap and elastic and you keep raw data for reprocessing.

Layers (the "medallion" or raw/staging/mart pattern):

  1. Raw/bronze: exact copy as landed (append only).
  2. Cleaned/silver: deduplicated, typed, conformed.
  3. Marts/gold: business-ready aggregates and star schemas.

Getting data out of OLTP:

  • Batch extract (nightly dump or incremental by updated_at): simple, misses hard deletes.
  • CDC (Debezium reading the WAL/binlog into Kafka): near real-time, captures deletes and every change.
  • Events published by services (clickstream, Kafka topics).

Orchestration: Airflow, Dagster or Prefect run DAGs with schedules, retries and dependencies; dbt manages SQL models and tests; data quality checks (row counts, null rates, freshness) gate downstream jobs.

# Airflow DAG sketch: nightly load then transform
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from datetime import datetime
with DAG("daily_orders", start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), schedule="0 2 * * *", catchup=False) as dag:
    load = BashOperator(task_id="load_raw", bash_command="python load_orders.py {{ ds }}")
    build = BashOperator(task_id="dbt_run", bash_command="dbt run --select marts.orders")
    load >> build

Idempotency matters. A rerun for the same day must not double-count. Load into a date partition and overwrite that partition, or MERGE by key. Late-arriving data: reprocess a window (for example last 3 days) every run.

Slowly changing dimensions (SCD). When a customer's city changes, SCD Type 2 keeps history by adding a new row with valid_from, valid_to, so last year's revenue is attributed to the old city.

Worked example. 300 GB/day of events. Landing as Parquet partitioned by dt=2026-11-09 costs ~$0.023/GB-month in S3 (about $7/day of new storage growth if kept in Standard). Nightly dbt build reads yesterday's partition (300 GB, 12 min on a medium warehouse), writes marts of 2 GB.

Industry examples. Airbnb (created Airflow), Netflix (Maestro, Iceberg), Uber (Hudi originated there), Spotify and Stitch Fix with dbt, Fivetran/Airbyte for managed connectors.

Decision gravity. Keeping raw data lets you change transformations later (reversible); transforming and discarding raw data is a one-way door. Schema changes upstream (renamed column) silently break pipelines, so use data contracts and tests.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen prep line: deliveries arrive (extract), are stored raw in the pantry (load), then washed, chopped and cooked to order (transform).

Common interview traps.

  • Non-idempotent jobs that double-count on retry.
  • Incremental loads by updated_at that miss deletes.
  • No freshness or quality monitoring, so dashboards quietly show stale numbers.

notes.title: Data lakes and the lakehouse
notes.html:
A data lake stores raw data of any shape (JSON, CSV, logs, Parquet, images) cheaply in object storage, to be read by many engines later ("schema on read"). A warehouse enforces structure on write ("schema on write").

Problem with a plain lake: it is just files. No ACID transactions, no easy updates/deletes (GDPR), no schema evolution, small-file problem, readers may see half-written data. It becomes a "data swamp".

Lakehouse table formats add a transaction log and metadata over Parquet files in object storage:

  • Apache Iceberg (Netflix origin), Delta Lake (Databricks), Apache Hudi (Uber origin).
  • Features: ACID commits, snapshot isolation, time travel (SELECT ... AS OF), schema evolution, row-level updates/deletes/upserts, hidden partitioning, compaction of small files.
  • Multiple engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake, BigQuery) can read the same tables.

File format choice: Parquet (columnar, compressed, the default for analytics) and ORC; Avro (row-based, good for Kafka and schema evolution); JSON/CSV only as raw landing.

Layout (Hive-style partitions):
s3://lake/orders/dt=2026-11-09/part-0001.parquet
s3://lake/orders/dt=2026-11-09/part-0002.parquet
Target file size: 128 MB to 1 GB. Thousands of 1 MB files = slow listing and planning.

Worked example. 1 PB lake in S3 Standard: 1,000,000 GB x $0.023 = $23,000/month; a comparable managed warehouse storage would cost more and tie you to one vendor. Compaction job merges 20,000 small files of 5 MB into 100 files of 1 GB, cutting query planning from 40 s to 3 s.

Industry examples. Netflix Iceberg tables on S3, Uber Hudi for upserts from CDC, Databricks lakehouse (Delta), Apple and Adobe on Iceberg, AWS Athena or Trino querying S3 directly.

Decision gravity. Warehouse for BI-heavy teams with SQL needs and low ops tolerance; lake/lakehouse for ML, unstructured data, multi-engine access and cost at petabyte scale. Open formats keep exit options (reversible). Many companies run both: lake as raw/system of record, warehouse for curated marts.

Everyday analogy. A lake is a big storeroom where you dump boxes of everything; a table format is the inventory ledger that tells you what is in which box and which boxes are current.

Common interview traps.

  • Dumping data in S3 with no catalog or schema, creating a swamp.
  • The small-files problem (millions of tiny Parquet files).
  • Ignoring deletes/GDPR on an append-only lake.

notes.title: Batch vs stream processing
notes.html:
Batch processes a large bounded dataset at intervals (hourly, nightly). Stream processes events continuously as they arrive (seconds or less).

Batch Stream
Data Bounded (yesterday's files) Unbounded (events forever)
Latency Minutes to hours Milliseconds to seconds
Throughput efficiency Very high Lower per record
Complexity Lower Higher (state, time, ordering, failures)
Examples Daily revenue report, ML training Fraud detection, live dashboards, alerts
Tools Spark, Hive, dbt, MapReduce Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming, Beam

Choose by the required freshness, not by fashion. Hourly freshness is often enough, and batch is cheaper and simpler.

Stream concepts senior interviews expect:

  • Event time vs processing time. Events arrive late or out of order (a phone offline in a tunnel). Use event timestamps.
  • Windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping, e.g. every 1 min), sliding (overlapping), session (gap-based).
  • Watermarks: the engine's estimate "no events older than T will arrive"; closes windows, with an allowed lateness for stragglers.
  • State: counts, joins and dedup need state, kept locally (RocksDB in Flink) and checkpointed to durable storage.
  • Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once (checkpointing plus transactional or idempotent sinks; Kafka transactions).
  • Backpressure: slow consumers must push back instead of crashing.
-- Flink SQL: orders per city per minute (tumbling window on event time)
SELECT city,
       TUMBLE_START(event_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS minute,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY city, TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE);

Worked example. Fraud check on card payments must decide within 200 ms: a stream job keeps a per-card 10-minute sliding count in state (about 1 KB per active card; 5M active cards = 5 GB state, sharded over 10 task slots). Nightly batch job recomputes models on 90 days of history (50 TB) and publishes updated thresholds.

Architectures.

  • Lambda: run batch and speed (stream) layers in parallel and merge at query time. Accurate but two codebases.
  • Kappa: everything is a stream; reprocess by replaying the log (Kafka with long retention). One codebase, needs a replayable log.
  • Streaming ingestion into a lakehouse (Flink or Spark writing Iceberg/Hudi) blends both: minutes of freshness, one storage layer.

Industry examples. LinkedIn built Kafka and Samza; Uber uses Flink and Pinot for live ops metrics; Netflix uses Flink for real-time recommendations and monitoring; Alibaba runs Flink at Singles' Day scale (billions of events/s reported); Spark remains dominant for batch ETL at most companies.

Decision gravity. Stream processing is a long-term operational commitment (state, upgrades, reprocessing). Start batch unless a product requirement (fraud, alerts, live UI) needs seconds. Moving batch to stream later is possible if sources are in Kafka and logic is idempotent; the reverse is easy.

Everyday analogy. Batch is doing all laundry on Sunday; streaming is washing each shirt the moment it gets dirty. Weekly laundry is more efficient; a pilot's shirt may need the second approach.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing streaming when daily batch meets the requirement.
  • Ignoring late and out-of-order events.
  • Claiming "exactly-once" end to end without idempotent or transactional sinks.
  • Forgetting how to reprocess history after a bug fix.

notes.title: Putting it together: an analytics architecture
notes.html:
A sensible end-to-end design for an e-commerce company at about 50M orders/year and 500M clickstream events/day:

  1. OLTP Postgres/MySQL for orders (sharded or not by size), DynamoDB for carts.
  2. CDC via Debezium into Kafka (8 to 24 partitions per big topic, 7 days retention); apps also publish clickstream events directly.
  3. Lake sink: Kafka Connect or Flink writes Parquet/Iceberg into S3, partitioned by dt and hour.
  4. Warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift) loads curated data; dbt builds star schemas daily and key marts hourly.
  5. Real-time layer: Flink aggregates for live dashboards and alerts, serving via Pinot/ClickHouse or Redis.
  6. Serving: BI tool (Looker, Superset), notebooks, ML feature store.
  7. Governance: catalog (DataHub, Glue), access control, PII masking, retention rules (GDPR deletion), lineage and data-quality tests.

Worked example (storage). 500M events/day x 500 bytes = 250 GB/day raw JSON; Parquet with compression is about 5x smaller: 50 GB/day, 18 TB/year, about $420/month in S3 Standard after one year of accumulation (18,000 GB x $0.023), and cheaper with tiering.

Cost levers. Partition and cluster tables, materialized aggregates, auto-suspend compute, cap runaway queries (BigQuery maximum_bytes_billed), tier old data to cold storage, and avoid duplicate copies.

Decision gravity. Each layer has an exit: raw events in open formats can be re-ingested into any warehouse. The commitment that is hardest to undo is business definitions ("what is an active user") scattered in dashboards; centralize them in a semantic layer or dbt models.

Industry examples. Common stacks: Fivetran/Airbyte + Snowflake + dbt + Looker; Kafka + Flink + Iceberg + Trino; Uber's Kafka + Hudi + Presto + Pinot.

Everyday analogy. A city's water system: reservoirs (lake), treatment plant (transform), taps for drinking (BI) and a fast pipe for firefighters (real-time).

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing every tool without justifying freshness and volume numbers.
  • Forgetting governance (PII, retention, access).
  • No plan for backfills and reprocessing.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• OLTP serves the app by key; OLAP scans history. Keep them on separate systems.
  • Column stores read only needed columns, compress well and vectorize; warehouses separate storage from compute; model with star schemas and prune partitions.
  • ELT with raw, cleaned and mart layers; make jobs idempotent, use CDC for deletes, test data quality, keep raw data.
  • Data lakes hold open-format files in object storage; Iceberg/Delta/Hudi add ACID, time travel and updates; fight small files.
  • Batch for hours-fresh and cheap; stream for seconds-fresh, with event time, windows, watermarks, state and delivery semantics.
  • Combine them (CDC, Kafka, lake, warehouse, real-time OLAP) based on freshness needs and cost, with governance built in.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP, and why not run reports on the production database?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A foundation for every data-architecture question; it shows whether you understand workload shape.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: OLTP serves the live app with many tiny key-based reads and writes at millisecond latency on a normalized row store. OLAP answers questions over history, scanning millions or billions of rows but few columns, on a columnar, denormalized store. A long scan on the production database evicts the cache, burns I/O and spikes latency for customers, so I copy data to a separate analytical system.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
OLTP OLAP
Touches 1 to 100 rows millions to billions of rows, few columns
Latency ms seconds to minutes
Layout row store column store
Schema normalized star schema

Worked example: a 2 TB orders table. WHERE id = ? reads one 8 KB page (1 ms). "Average order value per city, last 12 months" needs 3 columns over 500M rows; a row store reads about 2 TB, a column store about 60 GB, compressed to maybe 15 GB. A read replica is a first step but still row-oriented and shares engine limits. HTAP systems (TiDB, SingleStore) try both with trade-offs.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running reporting queries on the primary.
  • Believing one engine does both at large scale without trade-offs.
  • Forgetting a replica can lag and have replication conflicts with long queries.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do long queries on a replica hurt? -> In Postgres, conflicts with replay can cancel the query or delay replay unless tuned (verify settings).
  2. How does data reach the warehouse? -> Batch extract, or CDC (Debezium) via Kafka.
  3. Where do aggregates for a live dashboard belong? -> A real-time OLAP store (Pinot, ClickHouse) fed by a stream.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "OLAP is for analytics". The senior gives the I/O math, the layout reason and the isolation argument, and knows where read replicas stop being enough.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A finance dashboard with a 6-minute query on the primary pushed checkout p99 from 90 ms to 2 s at month-end.

questions.promptHtml: Why are column stores fast for analytics and slow for OLTP, and how does a cloud warehouse separate storage from compute?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests internal mechanisms (compression, vectorization, pruning) rather than product names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Analytics reads few columns of many rows, so storing each column together lets the engine read only what it needs, compress similar values 5 to 10x, process batches with SIMD and skip blocks via min-max metadata. Updating or fetching one whole row touches every column file, which is why OLTP suffers. Cloud warehouses keep columnar data in object storage and spin compute clusters up independently, so they scale and pause separately.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Row store   [1,Mumbai,250][2,Delhi,400][3,Mumbai,120]
Column store id: 1,2,3   city: Mumbai,Delhi,Mumbai (dictionary/RLE)   amount: 250,400,120

Techniques: dictionary, run-length, delta and bit-packing encoding; zone maps (min/max per block) to skip data; partitioning and clustering to prune; vectorized execution. Star schema: a fact table (orders) joined to small dimensions (date, customer). Separate storage and compute: Snowflake virtual warehouses, BigQuery slots, Redshift RA3. Pricing consequence: BigQuery on-demand charges per TB scanned (about $6.25/TB, verify), so SELECT * or missing partition filters cost real money.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT d.month, c.city, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_orders f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_id = d.date_id
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE d.year = 2026
GROUP BY d.month, c.city;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• SELECT * on columnar engines.
  • No partition pruning for daily reports.
  • Using a warehouse for high-concurrency point lookups.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do columns compress better? -> Same-type, often repetitive values sit together.
  2. What is a zone map? -> Per-block min/max that lets the engine skip blocks that cannot match a filter.
  3. Cost of separation of storage and compute? -> Network reads of remote data; mitigated by local caching.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "columnar is faster". The senior lists the five mechanisms, the pruning keys and ties them to the pricing model.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scheduled dashboard that scanned an unpartitioned 5 TB table daily was the top item in the monthly bill; adding a date partition cut it by 98%.

questions.contextHtml:
Every Monday 09:00 the checkout API p99 jumps from 120 ms to 3 s for about 8 minutes. Postgres primary (r6g.4xlarge, 2 TB orders table). Metrics at 09:02:

active connections: 310 (max 400)    cache hit ratio: 99.2% -> 71%
iowait 38%    longest running query: 7m 12s  "SELECT city, avg(total) FROM orders WHERE created_at > now() - interval '12 months' GROUP BY city"

A new weekly report by the analytics team runs at 09:00. The team proposes "just add an index on city".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds an index on city. The query still reads 500M rows of two columns; an index may not even be used, and it adds write overhead.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the report on the primary or a replica? How fresh must it be? Who else runs analytics? Do we have CDC or a warehouse?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Kill the query (pg_cancel_backend), move the schedule off peak, set statement_timeout for the reporting role.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: large scan evicts the buffer cache (hit ratio 99.2% to 71%); I/O saturation (iowait 38%); lock waits (unlikely for reads); connection pool exhaustion as a side effect (310 of 400).
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_activity, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a replica, pg_stat_statements, iostat -x.
  5. Root cause: OLAP work running on the OLTP primary: a 2 TB-scale sequential scan thrashed shared buffers and disk I/O for checkout queries.
  6. Fix: Short term: dedicated read replica with hot_standby_feedback tuned, role with timeout, scheduled off-peak. Long term: CDC to a warehouse (Debezium to Kafka to lake to BigQuery/Snowflake) and the report reads columnar data; build a mart city_revenue_daily.
  7. Prevention: Separate roles and connection limits for reporting, alert on queries over 60 s on the primary, a "no analytics on prod" review checklist.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A replica is cheap and fast to ship but replication conflicts can cancel long queries and the data stays row-oriented; I would not add an index "to fix the report" nor scale up the primary for it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Replica lag grows during the report? -> max_standby_streaming_delay vs cancellations (verify settings), or use a snapshot/logical replica.
  • Need results fresher than hourly? -> CDC into the warehouse or real-time OLAP.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a BI tool's "refresh all" button on the primary caused a recurring "mystery" incident every quarter-end.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds an index.
  • Hire: moves analytics off primary, uses a replica and timeout.
  • Strong hire: explains cache eviction and I/O, proposes CDC plus warehouse and guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
BigQuery on-demand bill is $9,400 this month, up from $1,100. Top query by bytes scanned:

SELECT * FROM analytics.events
WHERE JSON_VALUE(payload, '$.user_id') = '8812'

events is a 5 TB unpartitioned table, run 60 times a day by a support tool. Pricing about $6.25 per TB scanned (verify current).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy flat-rate slots" before fixing the query that scans the whole table.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does support need (one user's recent events)? Retention needed? Is user_id extractable into a column? Date range typical?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set maximum_bytes_billed on that service account and a project-level custom quota.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: SELECT * reads all columns; no partition or cluster pruning; JSON parsing prevents pruning; 60 runs per day multiplies it.
  4. Math: 5 TB x $6.25 = about $31 per run; 60 per day = $1,875/day; about $56k per month if all days; observed $9,400 means roughly 10 runs/day effective. After fix: partition by DATE(event_time), cluster by user_id (a real column), select 4 columns (about 5% of bytes), last 7 days (about 1/180 of rows): 5 TB x 0.05 x (7/365) = about 5 GB, $0.03 per run.
  5. Root cause: Full-table, full-column scans because the table layout does not match the access pattern.
  6. Fix: Materialize user_id as a column during ELT; create events_p partitioned and clustered; require a date filter (require_partition_filter = true); support queries go to a small per-user view; consider a search/OLTP store for per-user lookups.
  7. Prevention: Query cost dashboard by user, dry-run in CI (--dry_run) to show bytes, budget alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Slot reservations help for steady heavy use but don't fix waste; clustering costs reclustering on writes; I would not delete data to save money before fixing layout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the JSON filter bad? -> It requires reading the payload column for all rows; zone maps cannot prune.
  • Flat-rate pricing break-even? -> Compare steady monthly spend to slot price (verify); fix waste first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: one notebook with SELECT * in a loop cost more in a weekend than the whole team's monthly budget.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: buys capacity.
  • Hire: partition, cluster, column selection, quota.
  • Strong hire: shows math, require_partition_filter, dry-run guardrail, extracts JSON field.

questions.contextHtml:
Nightly job loads orders into the warehouse. Finance reports revenue 2x on days after a retry, and deleted (cancelled) orders still counted.

-- load_orders.sql, run by Airflow at 02:00 with retries=3
INSERT INTO warehouse.fact_orders
SELECT order_id, customer_id, total, updated_at
FROM source.orders
WHERE updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM warehouse.fact_orders);

The task failed at 02:40 after loading and was retried at 02:45. The source hard-deletes cancelled orders.
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug and give a corrected design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a DISTINCT." Doesn't handle deletes, late updates, or rerun semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is updated_at reliably set on all changes? Can orders update after delivery? Can we enable CDC? What is the freshness target?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Deduplicate yesterday's duplicates by order_id keeping the latest row, and restate affected reports.
  3. Hypotheses (bugs), ranked: plain INSERT is not idempotent (retry duplicates rows); MAX(updated_at) watermark skips rows with equal or late timestamps; updates produce duplicate versions rather than replacing; hard deletes never propagate.
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; anti-join with the source for deleted ids.
  5. Root cause: The job's output depends on its own prior state and prior runs, so reruns change the result.
  6. Fix: Load a bounded window into staging and MERGE by key, with a lookback to catch late rows; handle deletes via CDC tombstones or a soft-delete flag.
MERGE warehouse.fact_orders t
USING (SELECT * FROM source.orders
       WHERE updated_at >= TIMESTAMP '{{ ds }}' - INTERVAL '3 days') s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET total = s.total, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, customer_id, total, updated_at)
  VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.total, s.updated_at);

Better: partition overwrite per run date, so reruns replace the same partition. 7. Prevention: Data quality tests (unique order_id, row counts vs source, freshness) as a gate; idempotency review for every job. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The lookback window costs extra reads; CDC captures every change including deletes but adds infrastructure; I would not trust updated_at blindly where triggers or bulk updates bypass it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Data arrives 10 days late? -> Lookback of 10+ days or a reprocessing job triggered by a late-data marker.
  • Cheaper than MERGE at 300 GB/day? -> Overwrite the day's partition atomically.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a retried task doubled holiday revenue on the board dashboard and was found by a CEO, not by tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: DISTINCT.
  • Hire: MERGE or partition overwrite, handles deletes.
  • Strong hire: lookback window, CDC, data tests and reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: Operations lead: "We need real-time dashboards for orders." There are 40 ops staff, orders 20/s, and decisions are made every 15 to 30 minutes (staffing, courier allocation). The data team wants to adopt Flink and Pinot.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts designing a streaming cluster because the word "real-time" was used.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What decision changes if data is 10 seconds old vs 5 minutes old? Who acts and how fast? What's the cost of staleness? Alerts (automated) or humans looking? Accuracy vs speed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; I get a freshness SLO in writing: for example "orders per city visible within 2 minutes".
  3. Hypotheses (options): batch every 5 to 15 minutes (dbt incremental on CDC data); micro-batch/streaming ingestion into the warehouse or lakehouse (minutes); true streaming with Flink plus real-time OLAP (seconds).
  4. How I'd verify: Check with ops: a 2-minute delay does not change a 15-minute decision; 20 orders/s is about 1.7M/day, trivially handled by batch at 5 minutes.
  5. Recommendation: CDC into the warehouse with a 5-minute incremental model; a materialized view for the dashboard. Reserve streaming for requirements like fraud checks (under 1 s) or automated alerts.
  6. Fix (if truly needed later): Kafka plus Flink with event-time windows and a Pinot/ClickHouse serving layer.
  7. Prevention: Write freshness SLOs per dashboard and monitor them (max event timestamp age).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Streaming is a long-term operational commitment (state, reprocessing, upgrades); the cheaper design meets the requirement. If sources are already in Kafka and logic is idempotent, moving up later is possible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• They later add an alert "orders drop 50% in 1 minute"? -> That requirement justifies a small streaming job or a ClickHouse query on 1-minute rollups.
  • What does "real-time" cost in people? -> On-call for state recovery, schema changes and backfills.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a streaming dashboard had a 20 second latency target no one used; the team spent two quarters on a pipeline that a 5-minute batch would have matched.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: starts building Flink.
  • Hire: asks about decisions and freshness.
  • Strong hire: SLO first, batch/micro-batch recommendation with math, defined trigger for streaming.

questions.promptHtml: What problem do Iceberg, Delta and Hudi solve on top of Parquet files in object storage?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lakehouse is a mainstream interview topic; they want to see you understand why raw files are not enough.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A plain lake is just files: no transactions, no row-level updates or deletes, no safe schema change, and readers can see half-written data. Table formats add a transaction log or manifests over the Parquet files, giving ACID commits, snapshot isolation, time travel, schema evolution, upserts and compaction, and let several engines read the same tables.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
s3://lake/orders/dt=2026-11-09/part-0001.parquet     (data files, immutable)
s3://lake/orders/metadata/v123.json -> manifest list -> manifests -> data files   (Iceberg-style)

A commit atomically publishes a new metadata pointer, so readers see either the old or the new snapshot. Updates and deletes write new files plus delete files or rewrite files (copy-on-write vs merge-on-read). Time travel reads an old snapshot (SELECT ... AS OF). Compaction merges small files into 128 MB to 1 GB targets. Choice of formats: Parquet/ORC for columnar analytics, Avro for Kafka and schema evolution, JSON/CSV only as raw landing. Origins: Iceberg (Netflix), Hudi (Uber), Delta (Databricks).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dumping files into S3 with no catalog (data swamp).
  • Ignoring the small-files problem.
  • Ignoring GDPR delete needs on an append-only layout.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Copy-on-write vs merge-on-read? -> CoW rewrites files on update (fast reads, slow writes); MoR writes deltas merged at read or compaction (fast writes, slower reads).
  2. How do concurrent writers behave? -> Optimistic concurrency on the metadata pointer; conflicts retry or fail.
  3. Why open formats? -> Exit options and multi-engine access.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "Delta adds ACID". The senior explains snapshot publish, CoW/MoR, compaction and the catalog dependency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A GDPR deletion job on a raw S3 lake meant scanning and rewriting months of files until the team adopted a table format with row-level deletes.

questions.contextHtml:
A streaming job writes Parquet into s3://lake/events/dt=.../hour=.../ every 30 s from 40 tasks. After 3 months, a Trino query for one day went from 20 s to 6 minutes. Stats:

files for last 7 days: 2,350,000    avg size: 2.1 MB
query planning: 3m 10s    S3 LIST requests: 18,000    S3 503 SlowDown: sporadic

Storage cost is flat; data volume is about 120 GB/day.
questions.promptHtml: Explain and fix the performance, including how you avoid it recurring.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale up the Trino cluster." The bottleneck is listing and opening millions of tiny files, not compute.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which table format (plain Hive layout or Iceberg)? Freshness target for this table? Do readers need data within 30 s?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run an urgent compaction on the last 7 days' partitions (rewrite into 256 MB to 1 GB files), restrict queries to partitions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: small files (2.35M x 2.1 MB: 40 tasks x 2 files/min x 60 x 24 x ... many per partition); S3 list/GET overhead per file; planning cost scales with file count; partitioning too fine (hour plus others).
  4. How I'd verify: Count files and sizes per partition via aws s3 ls --summarize or Iceberg files metadata table; check Trino stats on splits.
  5. Root cause: Frequent commits from many parallel writers create files far below the target size; each query pays per-file overhead (listing, footer read, split planning).
  6. Fix: Short term: compaction job. Long term: write with larger commit intervals (checkpoint 5 to 10 minutes) or fewer writers, Iceberg/Hudi/Delta with automatic compaction, a manifest to avoid LIST calls, target 128 MB to 1 GB. Math: 120 GB/day at 512 MB is about 240 files per day, versus about 57,000 files per day today, a 200x reduction (from 7 days: 2.35M to roughly 1,700 files).
  7. Prevention: Monitor average file size and file count per partition; alert under 64 MB; scheduled compaction and snapshot expiry.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Bigger commit intervals increase data latency; compaction rewrites data (cost) and, in a plain Hive layout, races with readers unless the table format provides snapshots. I would not just buy a bigger cluster.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need 30 s freshness anyway? -> Keep a small-file hot layer for recent data and compact into the main table in the background (or serve recents from a real-time OLAP store).
  • Why did S3 503 appear? -> Request-rate pressure on prefixes from massive listings.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a table of 1 KB files made the metastore so slow that analysts blamed the warehouse for three weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale up the cluster.
  • Hire: compaction and bigger files.
  • Strong hire: file-count math, commit interval trade-off, table format auto-compaction, monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: A Flink job computes orders per city per 1-minute tumbling window on event time and feeds a live dashboard. Support: "Numbers are 4% lower than the nightly batch total, worse for rural cities." Job config: watermark = max event time minus 5 s, allowed lateness 0. Telemetry: mobile apps buffer events offline and upload in bursts; 6% of events arrive 30 s to 10 min late. Late-event metric: numLateRecordsDropped = 412,000 last 24 h.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without making the dashboard useless.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the watermark to 15 minutes." Latency of every window grows to 15 minutes for all cities.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the dashboard allowed to correct itself? What is the lateness distribution (p50, p99)? Do alerts use the same stream? Is the batch total the accepted truth?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Annotate the dashboard ("near-real-time, finalizes after 10 min"); enable a side output for late records so they are not lost.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: late records dropped after window close (matches 412k drops, 4% to 6%); clock skew; duplicates; windowing by processing time in some path.
  4. How I'd verify: Metrics for dropped late records per city; compare per-minute counts to batch; check event-time vs ingestion-time histogram.
  5. Root cause: Watermark assumed events are at most 5 s late; the data is not, so windows closed before stragglers arrived and allowed lateness 0 discarded them.
  6. Fix: Allowed lateness (for example 10 minutes) so windows update (retractions/upserts to a sink that supports update by key), side output for beyond-lateness records feeding a correction job, keep a lambda-style batch recompute nightly as the source of truth. Keep the primary watermark short (5 to 30 s) so the first answer stays fast, with updates later. Sink: upsert by (city, window_start) into Pinot/ClickHouse.
  7. Prevention: Alert when dropped-late fraction exceeds 0.5%; show "as of" timestamps; per-region watermark tuning (idle sources can stall watermarks, set idleness timeouts).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Larger lateness increases state size and memory; revisions to numbers surprise users; I would not delay all output for the slowest 6%.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• An idle partition stops the watermark? -> Configure source idleness so it does not hold back progress.
  • Exactly-once for the corrected counts? -> Idempotent upsert sink keyed by window.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after a stadium event, offline phones flushed their buffers and "yesterday's" orders appeared in today's windows, breaking the dashboard until event-time handling was fixed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases the watermark blindly.
  • Hire: allowed lateness plus late side output, event time concepts.
  • Strong hire: layered approach (fast approximate plus corrected), upsert sink, idleness, monitoring and batch reconciliation.

questions.promptHtml: What does "exactly-once" mean in stream processing, and why is end-to-end exactly-once harder than it sounds?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers are expected to reason about duplicates and failures, not repeat marketing terms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Delivery is at-most-once, at-least-once or exactly-once. Engines like Flink achieve exactly-once state updates with checkpoints, but the outside world only sees effects through sources and sinks. End to end it needs a replayable source, checkpointed offsets and either an idempotent sink (upsert by key) or a transactional two-phase-commit sink, otherwise a recovery can duplicate or lose output.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Source (Kafka offsets) -> operator state (RocksDB) -> sink
Checkpoint barrier: snapshot offsets + state atomically to durable storage
On failure: restore snapshot, rewind source, re-process records after the snapshot

Reprocessing after restore means a sink can receive the same records again. If the sink is idempotent (primary key upsert) duplicates are harmless; if it is transactional (Kafka transactions, two-phase commit committed on checkpoint completion) the partial output is aborted. An API call to a payment provider or an email is neither: it needs an idempotency key. Also note "effectively-once" is a better phrase: processing may repeat, effects are applied once. At-least-once plus idempotent writes is the pragmatic default.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming exactly-once while the sink is a non-idempotent HTTP call.
  • Counting with at-least-once and no dedup.
  • Not testing failure recovery.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cost of exactly-once? -> Checkpoint overhead, higher latency (commit on checkpoint), transaction timeouts.
  2. How to dedupe a Kafka consumer? -> Idempotent processing keyed by event id with a store, or transactional offsets and writes.
  3. What if the source is not replayable? -> Then exactly-once is not possible; buffer it in a log first.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "Kafka supports exactly-once". The senior describes the whole path, checkpoint barriers, idempotent vs transactional sinks and external side effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fraud-scoring job re-emitted decisions after a restore and customers received two SMS alerts until the sender used an idempotency key per decision.

questions.contextHtml: For 9 days the executive "active users" dashboard dropped 18% with no real change in behavior. Root cause found: an upstream team renamed user_id to account_id in the events topic. The bronze-to-silver job used SELECT user_id ... which evaluated to NULL for new data; a downstream COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) silently excluded NULLs. No tests failed, jobs were green. Raw data in the lake is intact. The nightly job takes 12 minutes for one day (300 GB).
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: fix, backfill, and prevent.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Tell the team to announce schema changes." No technical control or backfill plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tables and consumers are affected? Are marts rebuilt from raw or incrementally? Did anything snapshot bad numbers into reports/emails? Is there a schema registry?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Patch the silver model to COALESCE(account_id, user_id), annotate the dashboard, tell consumers about restated numbers.
  3. Hypotheses (contributing causes), ranked: no data contract or schema compatibility check; no null-rate test; silent NULL semantics in aggregates; no freshness-vs-volume-vs-distribution monitoring.
  4. How I'd verify: Null rate of user_id per day from raw vs silver (jumps from 0.01% to 100% on day X); compare daily distinct counts.
  5. Root cause: Unversioned upstream schema change plus pipeline code that tolerates NULL silently.
  6. Fix: Reprocess affected days from raw: because we kept bronze, backfill is idempotent partition overwrite for dt in the 9-day range (9 x 12 min = about 108 minutes sequential, less in parallel). Verify against expectations, then rebuild marts, then re-send restated reports.
  7. Prevention: Data contracts with a schema registry (backward-compatible changes only, CI check on producers), dbt tests (not_null, accepted ranges, row-count anomaly), anomaly detection on key metrics, lineage to find consumers, ownership and on-call for the dataset.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Strict contracts slow producers a little; fail-fast jobs may block pipelines (but better than wrong numbers). I would not patch only the dashboard query; and I would not hand-edit warehouse tables.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if raw data had been discarded after transform? -> A one-way door: backfill impossible; hence keep raw.
  • Fail pipeline or continue with warning? -> Fail for critical marts, warn for exploratory; tiered severity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a renamed column caused a 2 week silent revenue undercount, found by a finance analyst sanity-checking a quarterly report.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: process-only fix.
  • Hire: backfill from raw, add tests.
  • Strong hire: data contracts, anomaly monitoring, quantifies backfill, communicates restatement.

questions.contextHtml: A company has 80 TB in a proprietary-format cloud warehouse costing about $60k/month (compute $40k, storage $20k). Growth is 4 TB/month. A new ML team needs raw events (500M/day, about 250 GB/day JSON) and unstructured data; BI teams use SQL dashboards with 200 users. Compliance requires GDPR deletes within 30 days. Leadership asks whether to move to a lakehouse (Iceberg on S3 with Trino/Spark) and leave the warehouse.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend and how do you migrate?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lakehouse is modern and cheaper, migrate everything." No cost model, BI usability or risk staging.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Query concurrency and latency needs for BI? Team skills? Vendor contract and exit costs? Which workloads are expensive? Is ML the driver or cost?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; first understand cost drivers (storage vs compute, idle clusters).
  3. Hypotheses (options): stay and optimize; lakehouse only; hybrid: lake as system of record, warehouse for curated marts.
  4. How I'd verify: Storage math: raw 250 GB/day JSON becomes about 50 GB/day Parquet (5x), about 18 TB/year; 80 TB in S3 is about 80,000 GB x $0.023 = $1,840/month versus $20k in the warehouse storage line. But compute for 200 BI users on Trino needs sizing, and the ops cost is real.
  5. Recommendation: Hybrid. Land everything (CDC and events) in Iceberg on S3 as the raw/silver system of record and for ML; keep a managed warehouse (or serverless engine reading Iceberg) for gold marts and BI concurrency. This lets ML read open formats and keeps BI stable. Move large raw/history tables out of the warehouse first, where cost and ML pressure are highest.
  6. Fix (migration steps): (a) Dual-write: Kafka sink to Iceberg alongside the current pipeline. (b) Backfill history into Iceberg (export Parquet; checksum row counts). (c) Rebuild dbt models against Iceberg; reconcile outputs for 2 to 4 weeks. (d) Switch dashboards by domain. (e) Decommission warehouse tables. GDPR: row-level deletes via Iceberg with periodic compaction plus snapshot expiry so deleted data physically disappears inside 30 days.
  7. Prevention: Catalog and governance (access, PII masking, lineage), small-file compaction, cost monitoring.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Full cutover is risky for 200 BI users with trust in numbers; open formats make the decision reversible (keep an exit), a proprietary format would not. I would not migrate without reconciliation of outputs and would not forget governance, which warehouses give out of the box.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Warehouse can read Iceberg directly? -> Several engines can query external Iceberg tables (verify per vendor), which simplifies a hybrid.
  • Real-time needs? -> Add Flink into Iceberg for minute-level freshness or a real-time OLAP store.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team migrated all dashboards in one weekend, finance found 3% variance, and trust took months to rebuild; the next migration ran shadow dual-reporting.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-in cutover without numbers.
  • Hire: hybrid, storage cost math.
  • Strong hire: staged dual-run reconciliation, GDPR delete mechanics, open-format exit, governance and BI concurrency consideration.
